title: STL Algorithms
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs expect candidates to write erase-remove, custom-key sorts, binary-search bounds, and choose sort vs partial_sort vs nth_element correctly.

phases.goal: Establish that STL algorithms are free functions over half-open iterator ranges, parameterized by predicates and comparators.

must_hit.point: Almost all STL algorithms operate on a half-open range [first, last): first is included, last is past-the-end and must not be dereferenced; first == last is a valid empty range.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states half-open semantics, that end() is never dereferenced, and that passing end() as both bounds is a valid empty range.

must_hit.point: Algorithms are free functions decoupled from containers; they work through iterators rather than as container member functions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts member APIs with free functions in <algorithm> that take iterator pairs.

must_hit.point: Behaviour is parameterized by predicates: unary predicates (find_if, count_if, remove_if) take one element and return bool; binary predicates/comparators (sort, lower_bound) take two and must induce a strict weak ordering.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes unary vs binary callables and mentions strict weak ordering / operator< semantics.

must_hit.point: From C++20, many algorithms accept a projection applied to each element before the predicate/comparator; C++17 style uses a capturing lambda for the same effect.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate mentions proj / &Person::age with ranges::sort, or an equivalent capturing lambda comparator.

probes: What does the half-open range [first, last) mean for STL algorithms, and what goes wrong if you treat last as inclusive?
How do you pass a custom sort key or search condition to an STL algorithm?

hints.1: Think about where end() points and whether algorithms ever dereference it.
hints.2: Algorithms take two iterators and often a callable; classify that callable as unary predicate vs comparator.
hints.3: Answer shape: [first, last) includes first only; last is past-the-end; predicates/lambdas customize find_if/sort; never deref end().

phases.goal: Explain how core algorithm families actually behave: non-modifying queries, erase-remove, partitioning, sorting, binary search, heaps, and numeric folds.

must_hit.point: std::remove / remove_if / unique only relocate kept elements to the front and return a new logical end; they do not resize the container, so you must pair them with container erase (erase-remove idiom).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes v.erase(std::remove(...), v.end()) and explains algorithms are container-agnostic so they cannot call erase themselves.

must_hit.point: std::sort is not stable (~O(N log N)); stable_sort preserves relative order of equal elements; partial_sort puts the top K into final sorted positions in O(N log K); nth_element places the n-th order statistic with average O(N) and only partitions around it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate maps each algorithm to stability/partial-order guarantees and the stated complexities from the material.

must_hit.point: On a sorted range, lower_bound finds the first element not less than (≥) the value, upper_bound the first strictly greater, equal_range the [lower, upper) run, and binary_search only returns existence — all O(log N) with random-access iterators.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts boolean binary_search with iterator-returning lower_bound/equal_range and states the sorted precondition.

must_hit.point: std::partition reorders by predicate without preserving relative order (O(N)); stable_partition preserves order within each group; partition_point binary-searches the predicate boundary on an already-partitioned range (O(log N)).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes partition vs stable_partition and says partition_point is meaningless on an unpartitioned range.

must_hit.point: std::accumulate folds left with the init value’s type as the running type; std::reduce (C++17) may reorder/reassociate and needs a commutative associative op for a defined result.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate warns that accumulate(..., 0) can overflow in int and prefers 0LL when a wider sum is needed; contrasts ordered accumulate with reorderable reduce.

probes: Walk through the erase-remove idiom line by line: what does remove return, and why is erase still required?
When would you reach for nth_element instead of partial_sort or sort?
What is the difference between lower_bound and binary_search on a sorted vector?

hints.1: Algorithms only see iterators; ask what that implies for container size after remove.
hints.2: Separate “pack kept elements forward” from “truncate the container,” then map sort-family tools to top-K vs K-th element needs.
hints.3: Canonical form: v.erase(std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), pred), v.end()); top K ordered → partial_sort; only K-th/median → nth_element; existence → binary_search, position/count → lower_bound/equal_range.

phases.goal: Choose among sorting variants, partition flavors, accumulate vs reduce, and classic iterator APIs vs C++20 ranges based on guarantees and constraints.

must_hit.point: Need top K in order → partial_sort (O(N log K)); need only the K-th / median / unordered top K → nth_element (average O(N)); need a full stable multi-key sort → stable_sort or successive sorts from least to most significant key.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate picks the algorithm from the required ordering guarantee, not habitually calling full sort.

must_hit.point: Prefer accumulate when left-to-right order matters; prefer reduce / parallel transform_reduce only when the operation is commutative and associative and reordering is acceptable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate refuses reduce with floating subtraction or stateful left-to-right callables.

must_hit.point: partition is O(N) but does not preserve relative order; stable_partition preserves order and is O(N) with enough buffer or O(N log N) without.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate trades stability for speed/memory when explaining which partition to use.

must_hit.point: C++20 ranges let you pass the container directly (std::ranges::sort(v)) with optional projections and richer return types, but classic begin/end overloads remain what most interview whiteboards expect.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate can write both styles and notes projections as the C++20 alternative to hand-rolled comparators.

probes: You need the median of a large vector. Which algorithm and why not sort?
When is std::reduce the wrong choice compared to std::accumulate?

hints.1: Ask what ordering you actually need after the call returns.
hints.2: Compare full sort vs partial order vs single order-statistic placement; separately ask whether the fold may reorder.
hints.3: Median/K-th → nth_element average O(N); ordered top K → partial_sort; order-sensitive fold → accumulate; reorder-OK parallel fold → reduce.

phases.goal: Apply interview-ready idioms: erase-remove, custom comparators, sorted-range queries, permutation enumeration, and destination sizing for copying algorithms.

must_hit.point: Write the erase-remove (or erase-remove_if) one-liner from memory and explain that from C++20, std::erase / std::erase_if free functions wrap this for standard containers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate produces v.erase(std::remove_if(begin, end, pred), end) and mentions the C++20 wrappers.

must_hit.point: Sort or search by a custom key with a lambda comparator; prefer a named lambda or small functor when reused, and never use a floating-point comparator that can return true for both (a,b) and (b,a).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate shows sort(..., [](const T& a, const T& b){ return a.key < b.key; }) and states the broken-ordering trap.

must_hit.point: Classic CP pattern: sort ascending first, then do { … } while (next_permutation(...)) to enumerate all distinct permutations; starting unsorted misses earlier permutations and stops early.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate insists on sorting before the next_permutation loop.

must_hit.point: When writing to a destination range, pre-allocate enough space or use an inserter such as std::back_inserter; prefer four-iterator equal/mismatch (C++14) when second-range length is not obviously sufficient.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate avoids assuming copy/equal destinations are large enough and cites back_inserter or sized buffers.

probes: Write code to remove all even elements from a vector using the standard idiom.
How do you count occurrences of a value in a sorted vector without a linear scan?
Show how you would enumerate all permutations of a small array.

hints.1: Name the algorithm that “removes” without changing size, then the container call that finishes the job.
hints.2: For counts on sorted data, think equal_range + distance; for permutations, think sorted start + next_permutation loop.
hints.3: erase(remove_if(...), end); auto [lo,hi]=equal_range(...); distance(lo,hi); sort then do-while next_permutation.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Full std::sort (~O(N log N), not stable) when the whole range must be ordered. partial_sort when you need the top K elements in sorted order (O(N log K)). nth_element when you only need the K-th / median or an unordered partition around that rank (average O(N)).
partition is O(N) and may scramble relative order within each side. stable_partition keeps relative order within groups; it is O(N) with enough buffer and O(N log N) if extra memory is unavailable.

accumulate is a left fold whose init type is the running type—use when order matters. reduce (C++17) may reorder/reassociate for parallelisation, so the op should be commutative and associative; otherwise prefer accumulate.

binary_search only answers existence. Use lower_bound for the first ≥ insertion/match point, upper_bound for first >, and equal_range for the equal run / count—on a range already sorted with the same comparator.

tradeoffs.topic: Classic iterator-pair algorithms vs C++20 std::ranges
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Ranges accept the container directly, support projections, and return richer result types, but classic begin/end overloads remain valid and are what most interview whiteboards still expect.

gotchas.trap: Treating last as inclusive or dereferencing end()
gotchas.correction: Ranges are half-open [first, last); last is past-the-end and never dereferenced. Off-by-one bugs usually come from treating last as inclusive.

gotchas.trap: Assuming std::remove / remove_if / unique shrink the container
gotchas.correction: They only pack kept elements forward and return the new logical end; always pair with container erase (or C++20 std::erase / erase_if).

gotchas.trap: Three-iterator equal / mismatch when the second range may be shorter
gotchas.correction: Those overloads assume the second range is at least as long as the first; a shorter second range is undefined behaviour—prefer the four-iterator C++14 overloads.

gotchas.trap: Using std::random_shuffle or unique without sorting
gotchas.correction: random_shuffle is removed in C++17—use std::shuffle with an explicit engine such as mt19937. unique only collapses consecutive duplicates; sort first if needed.

gotchas.trap: Calling binary_search / lower_bound on an unsorted range, or using binary_search when you need a position
gotchas.correction: Sorted/partitioned precondition is required; unsorted input yields wrong answers in practice. binary_search is existence-only—use lower_bound or equal_range for where/how many.
The init argument’s type is the accumulation type: accumulate(..., 0) stays in int even for large ints or vector<long long>. Pass 0LL / 0.0 / a typed zero matching the desired result.

gotchas.trap: Using reduce / parallel transform_reduce with non-associative or stateful ops
gotchas.correction: reduce may reorder operations—avoid non-associative ops (e.g. floating subtraction) and stateful left-to-right callables; prefer accumulate when order matters.

gotchas.trap: Confusing std::move the algorithm with std::move the cast
gotchas.correction: The algorithm (#include <algorithm>) move-assigns a range into a destination; source elements are left valid but unspecified. The cast lives in <utility>.
search finds the first contiguous subsequence match; find_end finds the last. find_first_of matches any value from a set of keys, not a contiguous subsequence.

gotchas.trap: Parallel execution policies with unsafe callables
gotchas.correction: With par / par_unseq, element access and user callables must be thread-safe; overlapping mutation is a data race, and exceptions from parallel algorithms may call std::terminate.
